title: The Linux Filesystem Tree 🌳
description: Understand the hierarchical structure: root, home, and the big picture.

slides.title: Everything is a File (or Folder) 🗃️
slides.content:
## The Grand Tree

In Linux and macOS, the filesystem is organised like an upside‑down tree. The very base is the **root directory**, written as a single slash `/`.

- Everything – your documents, system files, even devices – lives somewhere under `/`.
- Directories (folders) can contain files or other directories.
- No drive letters like `C:` – all disks are mounted somewhere under the root.

Think of `/` as the Earth, and every folder is a continent, country, or city.

quizData.question: What symbol represents the root directory in Linux?
quizData.explanation: The root directory is a single forward slash `/`. It's the top of the filesystem tree.

slides.title: Your Home Sweet Home 🏠
slides.content:
## Home Directory

Every user has a personal folder inside `/home/` (Linux) or `/Users/` (macOS). This is your **home directory**, where you store your personal files.

- Symbolised by `~` (tilde).
- If your username is `alice`, your home is `/home/alice`.
- When you open a terminal, you normally start in your home directory.

slides.title: Where Am I? 📍
slides.content: Use `pwd` to see your current directory. Try it now!

quizData.question: What shortcut symbol stands for your home directory?
quizData.explanation: The tilde `~` is shorthand for the current user's home directory.

slides.title: Important Top‑Level Folders 🗺️
slides.content:
## The Big Picture

Some directories you'll see right under `/`:

- `/bin` – essential command binaries (like `ls`, `cp`).
- `/etc` – system configuration files.
- `/home` – users' personal homes.
- `/tmp` – temporary files (cleared on reboot).
- `/var` – variable data like logs.

You don't need to memorise them all now. Just know they're part of the tree.

slides.title: Pro Tip 🚀
slides.content:
## Visualise the Tree
Run `tree /` (if installed) to see a beautiful ASCII art of the entire filesystem. Use `tree ~` to start from home.
